name: Wigs and hairpieces

card.summary: Wigs, lace fronts and toupees add or replace hair instantly, giving a fuller head of hair and a changed hairline without treatment or surgery.
card.note: Quality, fit and natural-looking hairlines vary widely between products.

quick.overview:
Wigs and hairpieces cover hair loss or thin hair immediately. They change how full the hair looks and where the hairline sits, and a hand-tied or lace-front design is made so hair appears to grow from the skin.

Wigs have a long history, from ancient Egypt to the powdered wigs of the 18th century, and today are used by people with alopecia, cancer patients, and men and women with pattern hair loss. A dermatology review notes that wigs may reduce stigmatisation and improve self-esteem and social confidence, while also noting that the medical literature on wigs is not extensive.
quick.how: Options include machine-stitched weft wigs (the most widely worn), hand-tied lace wigs and lace fronts, in human or synthetic hair. Fibres, foundations and attachment methods differ, and custom colour and texture matching is common in higher-priced products.
quick.risks: Reported issues are mostly cosmetic or skin-related: heat and friction under the base, allergy to fabrics or adhesives, and, in one published case report, skin depigmentation linked to wig wearing. Attachment methods and care affect comfort and appearance.

lead: Wigs and hairpieces are artificial hair coverings worn to add volume, restore a hairline or change style. They are used for baldness, chemotherapy-related hair loss, alopecia areata, religious or professional reasons, protective styling, and entertainment [1][7]. The change is immediate: a wig or hair system alters the visible hairline, density, length and colour the moment it is put on, without waiting for medication or surgery to take effect.

In looksmaxxing forums, wigs and 'hair systems' come up as an immediate option for men whose hair is thin or receding, with some posters describing premium custom human-hair units as the only way to get a fuller look in their case, and others describing hair as a decisive feature in attraction [2].

Wigs have a long history, from Egyptian wigs that shielded shaved heads from the sun to the powdered periwigs of 17th- and 18th-century European courts, and the toupée industry that peaked in the United States in the mid-twentieth century [1][6]. A 2021 dermatology review describes wigs as helping to minimise the psychological consequences of hair loss, reducing stigmatisation and improving social confidence, self-esteem and quality of life, while noting that the medical literature on them is limited [3].

angle.text: A wig replaces or adds hair on the spot, so the visible hairline and density change without waiting for medication or surgery. Custom-colour, hand-tied units are used to appear natural.

paras: Machine-stitched weft wigs, with hair sewn onto a stretch weft, are the most widely worn. Hand-tied lace wigs knot each strand into French or Swiss lace, and lace-front wigs use fine flesh-coloured lace at the front so hair seems to grow from the skin [1]. Wikipedia describes the older weft method, in which hair roots are sewn onto silk thread and attached to a net foundation, and the ventilating or knotting method developed in the 19th century, in which a fine hook knots a few strands at a time into the foundation, giving a lighter and more natural look common in custom, film and theatre wigs [1].

Human hair includes 'Remy' hair with intact, aligned cuticles that reduce tangling; European hair is the most expensive and rare [1]. Synthetic fibre is made in the required colours and has no directional growth to manage [1]. Wikipedia notes that cheaper wigs use chemically processed hair with the cuticle stripped, whereas better ones keep the hair's growth direction aligned, a process called turning [1].

Men's toupées and hair systems are usually custom-made from synthetic or human hair, with quality versions sewing each strand onto fine, flesh-coloured lace [6]. Attachment is most commonly by adhesive, with elastic bands in cheaper versions and hair weaves, in which the base is woven into natural hair, popular in the 1980s and 1990s but associated with discomfort and traction alopecia [6]. A very thin piece applied with medical adhesive and worn for weeks is described as non-surgical hair replacement [6].

Ancient Egyptians wore wigs to shield shaved heads from the sun, fixing them with beeswax and resin, and Assyrians, Greeks and Romans also wore them [1]. Use largely lapsed in the West for around a thousand years, then revived in the 16th century for hair loss and lice; Queen Elizabeth I wore a red wig [1]. Louis XIII began wearing wigs in 1624 after going prematurely bald, Louis XIV helped spread the fashion across Europe in the 1660s, and after Charles II's return in 1660 periwigs became fashionable at the English court [1]. A wigmakers' guild was founded in France in 1665 [1].

Powdered wigs dominated men's fashion for about 140 years until a 1795 British hair powder tax effectively ended the fashion [1]. Wikipedia says wig-wearing was waning by 1765 outside some occupations and was revived briefly in the 1770s Macaroni period, and that only four US presidents, John Adams through James Monroe, wore powdered wigs in office [1]. In the 1960s modacrylic fibre made wigs more affordable [1].

Wikipedia says the toupée developed in the 18th century and gained a US following in the 19th, and that from 1954 several makers advertised in major magazines and newspapers, with Max Factor credited for higher-quality, nearly invisible pieces [6]. By the 1950s an estimated 350,000 US men wore hairpieces, and Time estimated US sales at 15 million dollars a year in 1959 and more than 2.5 million wearers by 1970 [6]. Wikipedia lists wearers including John D. Rockefeller, who began wearing them after alopecia in 1901, Bing Crosby, Gary Cooper, Groucho Marx and, per a 2010 auction, John Wayne [6].

Toupées have long been a subject of humour, with an 1837 George Cruikshank illustration cited as an early example, and Wikipedia reports that new male orders at the Japanese wigmaker Aderans fell 30 percent between 2002 and 2004 and that growing acceptance of shaved heads and drug and transplant options reduced use [6]. Finasteride and minoxidil were FDA-approved in the 1990s [6][7].

A hair prosthesis, or cranial prosthesis, is a custom wig fitted to people who have lost hair to conditions such as alopecia areata, alopecia totalis, trichotillomania or chemotherapy; Wikipedia says doctors have prescribed them since the 1950s and that the base is made of hypoallergenic fabric for sensitive skin [8]. The term is used when applying for medical insurance or tax-deduction status [8].

Reviews report that 47 percent of female chemotherapy patients consider hair loss the most traumatic aspect of treatment, that about 8 percent would decline chemotherapy for fear of it, and that chemotherapy-induced hair loss has an estimated incidence of 65 percent [10][11]. The Cochrane review of alopecia areata notes that the condition affects roughly 0.15 percent of the population and that hair loss can have a severe social and emotional impact [12].

For male pattern hair loss, Wikipedia reports that about half of men have pattern hair loss by age 50, lists hats, wigs and toupées among alternatives to drugs and transplants, and notes quality varies widely, with the best wigs costing tens of thousands of dollars in the US [7]. Two meta-analyses cited by Wikipedia found average psychosocial distress from hair loss to be moderate and no higher rates of depression among balding men [7].

On looksmax.org, one member who had finished a surgery path described thin hair as his biggest remaining facial flaw, said a hair transplant would still leave his hair thin, and was considering a custom human-hair wig, with colour and texture custom, priced over 1,000 euro and meant for evening wear, while noting concern about the vendor having no reviews and not replying to enquiries [2]. A reply in the same thread said the topic should stay pinned because members needed to advance their knowledge of male wig products, and listed good thickness, slight wave, good length and a Norwood 0 hairline as attractive male hair features from a female perspective [2].
Such threads reflect interest in non-surgical alternatives to transplants and medication, with a focus on realistic hairlines and custom colour matching [2].

A randomised trial examined hypoallergenic fabrics in medical wigs for women with chemotherapy-induced alopecia [4]. A case report in the British Journal of Dermatology described leucoderma secondary to wig wearing [5]. Wikipedia reports that hair weaves attached to natural hair can cause discomfort and traction alopecia from repeated tightening [6].

Wigs sit alongside other ways of changing hair appearance: minoxidil and finasteride, hair transplantation, scalp micropigmentation, comb-overs, hats and shaving the head [7][6]. For chemotherapy, scalp cooling devices are studied as a way to reduce hair loss, for example the 2017 SCALP randomised trial in breast cancer patients [13][10].

Research is mostly on medical wigs for hair loss. A 2021 review covers synthetic and custom hair systems, fibres, foundations and attachment methods, and reports psychological benefits of wigs for people with alopecia [3]. A randomised clinical trial studied improved hypoallergenic fabrics in medical wigs for breast cancer patients with chemotherapy-induced alopecia [4]. No trials examine wigs for cosmetic improvement in men without a medical diagnosis.

timeline.event: Egyptians wear wigs, partly to shield shaved heads from the sun; Grokipedia dates their origin to around 3400 BC [1][9].
Wigs revive in Europe for hair loss and lice [1].
Louis XIII begins wearing wigs after premature baldness [1].
A wigmakers' guild is founded in France [1].
British hair powder tax effectively ends the powdered-wig fashion [1].
Doctors begin prescribing hair prostheses; US toupée advertising grows from 1954 [8][6].
Time estimates US hairpiece sales at 15 million dollars a year [6].
Modacrylic synthetic fibre makes wigs cheaper [1].
Finasteride and minoxidil gain FDA approval, offering drug alternatives to hairpieces [6].
A Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology review summarises wig types and psychological benefits [3].

lore.intro: Wigs appear in hair-loss threads as an immediate alternative to transplants or medication, and members debate vendors and realism [2].

claims.claim: A custom real-hair wig can fix thin hair when a transplant would not
claims.believers: One poster argued that even a transplant would leave his hair thin and that a custom real-hair wig was his only solution [2].
claims.experts: A dermatology review describes wigs as offering immediate cosmetic results and psychosocial benefit for alopecia patients [3].

claims.claim: Hair thickness and hairline are decisive for attraction
claims.believers: A looksmax.org reply says hair is a fundamental feature in attraction and lists thickness, a slight wave, length and a Norwood 0 hairline [2].
claims.experts: Wikipedia cites two meta-analyses that found average psychosocial distress from balding to be moderate, without higher depression rates among balding men [7].

claims.claim: Wigs reduce the stigma of hair loss
claims.believers: Wearers with hair loss describe wigs as restoring a normal appearance and confidence, as summarised in the review [3].
claims.experts: The 2021 review says wigs may reduce stigmatisation and improve self-esteem, while noting limited literature [3].

claims.believers: The thread's original poster considered a lace-front-style premium unit with custom colour and texture, valuing realism above price [2].
claims.experts: Wikipedia says quality varies widely and notes lace fronts are made so hair seems to grow from the scalp [7][1].

claims.claim: Wigs are risk-free compared with surgery
claims.believers: Users frame wigs as a non-surgical option that avoids transplant limits [2].
claims.experts: A case report links wig wearing to leucoderma and Wikipedia reports traction alopecia with woven attachments [5][6].
